references.text: The preceding verse presents the contrast: the people and tax collectors gave God justice and were baptized with John's baptism, while the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected God's plan.

Jesus asks the chief priests and elders whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men. They refused to answer, revealing their rejection of John's authority—parallel to the Pharisees' rejection in Luke 7:30.
Jesus says that John came in the way of righteousness, but tax collectors and prostitutes believed him, while the religious leaders did not repent—the same contrast found in Luke 7:29-30.
Jesus asks a question about John's baptism and whether it was from heaven or from men. The religious leaders refused to take a stand, showing their rejection of God's counsel through John.
Wisdom is justified by all her children—a summary that implicitly contrasts those who received John and Jesus with the Pharisees who rejected God's plan.
Paul says he has proclaimed the whole counsel (βουλή) of God without holding anything back—the same expression 'God's counsel/plan' (τὴν βουλὴν τοῦ θεοῦ) that the Pharisees rejected.

Paul and Barnabas tell the Jews who reject the message that they push God's word away from themselves and judge themselves unworthy of eternal life—parallel to how the Pharisees rejected God's counsel 'against themselves' (εἰς ἑαυτούς).
Wisdom says she called and stretched out her hand, but no one would listen, and they rejected all her advice—a thematic parallel to the Pharisees' rejection of God's counsel.

Woe to the rebellious children who carry out a plan that is not from the Lord—an Old Testament example of rejecting God's counsel and following their own will, parallel to the attitude of the Pharisees.
John warns the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism and calls them a brood of vipers—this already shows the tension between John and the Pharisees regarding baptism.

Jesus pronounces woe upon the lawyers because they took away the key of knowledge; they did not enter themselves, and they hindered those who wanted to enter—parallel to how the lawyers rejected God's counsel for themselves.
